title: The International Pipeline Edge
subtitle: Why some organizations consistently extract better ERA outcomes from acquired pitchers — and what the roster data says about why

sections.content:
When you trade for a pitcher, you are not just acquiring a player. You are acquiring a player into a context. The coaching staff, the development infrastructure, the bullpen he works beside — all of it shapes what he becomes on the other side of the transaction.

Most trade models ignore this. They score the pitcher and ignore the receiver. This one doesn't.

A Bayesian regression across 632 pitcher acquisitions from 2010 through 2024 surfaced a persistent, non-obvious finding: the share of international-born pitchers already on the acquiring roster is one of the strongest predictors of post-trade ERA improvement — across FIP, xFIP, and SIERA simultaneously.

The coefficient clears the D-26 credibility threshold — directional mass ≥ 97.5%, 90% CI excludes zero — independently on all three metrics. That is not common. Most features that look credible on one ERA metric fade on the others. This one doesn't fade.

sections.title: The finding
sections.content: Each standard deviation increase in a team's international-born pitcher share is associated with a 0.034–0.073 standard deviation improvement in acquired pitcher ERA metrics, holding player quality constant. The effect is consistent across the full 2010–2024 sample and the 2021–2024 holdout.

The chart below shows team-level aggregates: each dot is one franchise, plotted by its mean international-born pitcher share against the mean FIP delta for pitchers it acquired from 2010–2024. The regression line is the posterior mean. Teams below zero on the y-axis got better FIP from acquired pitchers than those pitchers posted before the trade.

sections.title: International roster share vs acquired pitcher FIP improvement (team-level, 2010–2024)
sections.caption: Each dot is one franchise (min. 5 pitcher acquisitions). Dot size = number of acquisitions. Reference line at y=0: pitchers above the line declined on FIP post-trade; below improved. The regression slope is negative — more international pipeline, better ERA outcomes.

sections.content:
The relationship is noisy at the team level — as you'd expect from 14 years of roster turnover and variable trade quality. But the Bayesian model, which controls for the quality of the acquired pitcher, the receiving team's age profile, and several other contextual features, surfaces the international share signal cleanly and consistently.

The most natural mechanism: organizations that attract, develop, and retain a higher share of international pitchers have built infrastructure that transfers to any pitcher they acquire. Bilingual coaching. Biomechanics staff with international experience. A culture of technical development that doesn't depend on a player coming through a standard American developmental pathway.

A plausible alternative: this is a market-size confound. Large-market teams both sign international talent and have better support infrastructure. Atlanta, Toronto, and Los Angeles all have above-median international shares and strong pitching development reputations — and all three land below zero on FIP delta in this sample.

sections.title: The confound worth testing
sections.content: The most important robustness check is payroll-stratified: does the international share effect survive within payroll quintile? If high-payroll teams are driving both the international share and the ERA improvement, the feature is a proxy for market size, not development capacity. This check has not yet been run. Treat this finding as a strong prior to investigate, not a conclusion.

What this means in practice depends on whether the confound survives scrutiny. If the effect is real and not entirely explained by payroll, it suggests that acquiring organizations with deep international pitcher infrastructure are systematically underpriced in trade markets — because conventional trade evaluation focuses on the pitcher's history, not the receiver's context.

The data can't answer this yet. But it is pointing somewhere specific enough to follow.

methodology_note: V3 Bayesian regression (Student-t likelihood, ν≈4) fit on 2010–2020 training data, evaluated on 2021–2024 holdout. Feature: receiver_pct_international_born (mean share of international-born pitchers on the acquiring team in the trade season). Outcomes: FIP delta, xFIP delta, SIERA delta (post-trade minus pre-trade, normalized within position class and era). Credibility threshold: directional mass ≥ 97.5%, 90% CI excludes zero. All three outcomes clear this threshold independently.
